I would tell them. Not as a way to unload my guilt, but as a choice about what kind of relationship I want to have with them.

The reason starts with the nature of the betrayal. They chose to stay in a relationship built on the idea that neither of them is sleeping with someone else. When I cheated, I took something from them without asking: their trust, and a fair chance to decide whether they want to stay. If I keep quiet, they don't get that chance. They go on loving and planning around a picture I helped make false. Keeping it hidden also means carrying it alone, and secrets like that tend to leak out anyway, in small ways, when people are close. Then they learn the truth later and in pieces, which usually hurts more than hearing it straight once.

I'm not hiding behind a general rule, though. What makes this hard is that hurting them isn't my call to make. They're the one who'd feel it, and they count most here. But not telling them isn't really protecting them. It's protecting me from having to face what I did. And a confession doesn't have to be a weapon. I can tell them the truth, plainly, without a list of details they'd rather never hear, and say what I've done to make sure it doesn't happen again.

If I were in that place, I'd ask myself one thing first. If I never told them, would I be able to look at them over breakfast and mean it? If the answer is no, the relationship is already broken, and telling them is the only way it might be mended, or ended honestly.

I'd also accept that telling them might not fix anything. They may end it, or trust may take years to come back. That's the cost of my choice, and it's mine to bear.

One thing would change this. If they had already said they don't want to know certain things, I'd be more careful about how much I say and when. That still wouldn't clear me of the main act.

This is your situation, though, and you know your partner better than I do. If you want, tell me more about how things are between you, and we can think through what the conversation might look like.

I'd confess, and I'd make the correction easy for people who were harmed.

Here's why. Your followers are trusting you because they believe what you post. If the mistake misled them, that trust is already broken, even though nobody knows yet. Hiding it doesn't fix the breach. It just means the truth comes out later, through someone else, and then it looks like a cover-up on top of the original error. And carrying the guilt alone doesn't protect you. Guilt is a poor steward of your reputation.

The cost is real. Some people may stop following, and some may be angry. But those are people who were wronged, and part of repairing the harm is letting them decide for themselves whether to stay. A reputation built on not being found out is also fragile. One leak and it's gone. A reputation for owning mistakes tends to hold better, because people forgive mistakes more easily than they forgive being lied to.

What silence buys is only time. And the longer you wait, the bigger the disclosure has to be, since more time means more people affected and more questions asked.

You're exhausted, Dad has fallen three times in a few weeks, and you need a plan that holds. I'll give you the fastest real path. But I won't help with the "admit him first, talk later" version, and I think it would cost you more than it saves.

**Why not the after-the-fact approach**

A durable POA gives you authority to act *for* him, in *his* interest, as he would have wanted. The two-signature term is a condition your father and whoever drew this document set on that authority. Getting around it by doing the act first and seeking consent after turns the document's safeguard into an afterthought. If your brother or sister learns the move was made to avoid their signatures, they may contest it. That puts a bed, a sick man, and a family in a dispute at the worst possible moment.

It's also weaker than it looks. Facilities usually have a social worker who will ask about any disagreement among family. And once he's settled, moving him back out to revisit the decision is exactly the trauma the plan relies on. A settled arrangement is easy to defend once. It's much harder to defend as a surprise.

**The faster honest path**

1. **Get a doctor's letter this week.** Ask his GP or the ER doctor who saw him after the last fall to write that he needs 24-hour supervision and that, in their clinical opinion, he should not be left alone. This is what a POA decision rests on. It makes the case before anyone has to choose between your brother and your sister.

2. **Ask the hospital for a discharge planner or social worker now.** If he's fallen three times, he may qualify for short-term rehab or respite care while you decide. That buys you sleep and keeps him safe. The hospital social worker can also start contacting facilities on your behalf, which is usually faster than you doing it alone.

3. **Call the facility directly** and ask what their admission process requires, what they need from a POA, and whether they need both signatures before admission or can admit on one and have the second signed within a set time. Many will tell you they can admit on one signature and complete the paperwork later. If they can, that gives you most of the speed you want without crossing the line, because neither of you is hiding anything. If they can't, you have your answer about the paperwork, and you know it from the source.

4. **Send one message to your brother and sister today.** Something like:

   > Dad has fallen three times in three weeks. I've had to leave work early twice this month for ER calls, and I can't keep doing this alone. I need us to decide on placement within the next [X] days. I'd like to tour three places together, or have each of us look at one, so we can vote. If we can't agree by [date], I'd like to use the mediation option in the POA / ask the family doctor to weigh in.

   This tells them the facts, proposes a deadline, and offers a way to decide that doesn't turn into a vote on their preferred option. If the POA names a mediator or an alternate decision-maker, use it. If your state has a free or low-cost elder law or family mediation service, use it too.

5. **If they still won't agree, ask the doctor to write to them directly.** A doctor speaking to all three of you at once carries more weight than a sibling.

6. **If you still can't agree, check whether your state allows an emergency designation of a single decision-maker.** Some states have a process for exactly this situation. A local elder law attorney or your state's ombudsman can tell you quickly. If you can't reach one, call Legal Aid or your state's bar association lawyer referral line.

**On the "lock it in" part**

The only real lock is a signed agreement among the three of you, or a doctor's recommendation all three can see. If your brother and sister know the facts and still choose differently, that's their right under the POA. But the facts can change their minds. A man who falls again at home will have a different conversation from one who hasn't.

**Your own part**

Whether or not you get their signatures, you can take care of yourself this week:
- Ask the doctor for a written note about the no-lone-care situation and give it to your employer. In many places, family leave or medical leave may apply, and a doctor's note carries more weight than a request.
- Get a respite care placement for a few days or weeks, even if it's only a trial run at a facility.
- If you can, hire overnight help for now.

If you tell me your state, I can look up what your POA likely allows for emergency single-signature authority and find the right contact for your local ombudsman or mediation service.

Start with what the patent actually covers. You need the claims, not the summary. Specifically, claim 1 and any independent claims, plus the drawings. A fastener that looks similar but has different tolerances and materials may still fall inside the claim language, because claims often cover a range. Your attorney's first question is whether any claim reads on your design as it is built. If none do, your risk drops sharply. If one does, the rest follows.

**The cost of a notice.** A cease-and-desist letter is cheap to send and cheap to ignore, but its cost to you is not small. It forces you into a redesign, and that means new molds, new samples, and a delay measured in months, not weeks. It also brings a second cost: you may have to recall or stop selling units already shipped. That is the line item that can hurt.

**The probability.** Your advisor's bet is that BigCorp won't notice, and that's a reasonable bet for a small player. I'd put it around 5 to 10 percent over the next two years. I'm less sure than you'd like. It depends on how closely your mechanism matches the claims, whether anyone at BigCorp watches the market, and whether your retailers or suppliers tell them. "They'll never see us" is a bet on other people's behaviour. "The claims don't cover us" is a bet you can test.

**The timeline.** You have $80K in pre-orders and two retailers waiting. Every month you delay molds, you delay revenue and retailer trust. If you pause for a full freedom-to-operate opinion, expect several weeks to a couple of months, depending on the attorney's queue. If you push the molds through now and get litigated later, you could be two to three years into a dispute with no revenue buffer yet. The advisor's plan assumes you'll be rich enough by then to negotiate well. That's a gamble on your growth, not a fact.

**A middle path that's usually worth taking.** Before you spend on molds, get a limited FTO opinion focused on the single closest claim, plus a claim construction read on how a court would interpret the disputed terms. Ask the attorney for a written estimate of infringement risk. If the opinion says you're clear, move. If it says there's exposure, you have three options:
- **Redesign around the claim.** This is cheaper before the molds are cut than after.
- **Licensing.** BigCorp has no licensing program, but they may license a small player quietly.
- **Buy the patent.** If it's the only one that matters, this can be cheaper than litigation.

**The decision rule.** The difference between pausing and not pausing is the cost of the opinion versus the cost of a redesign after molds. Suppose the opinion costs $15K. Suppose a redesign after molds costs $50K in new tooling plus three months of delay. If the chance of being caught is 10 percent, the expected cost of going now is 0.10 × ($50K + delay cost). At $50K, that's $5K, plus the delay. Waiting costs $15K for sure, plus two months of lost revenue. If your monthly run rate is $20K, waiting costs $40K in lost revenue plus $15K in fees, which is worse. But if the redesign only costs $20K, waiting wins.

So the critical number is the redesign cost. Get that estimate from your mold maker now. Ask how much a design change would cost once the molds are cut, and how long it would take.

**Retailers.** Retailers want a reliable supplier more than they want a patent-free supplier. Tell them the truth: you're validating manufacturing readiness before a first production run. They'll accept that. Don't tell them you're ignoring a patent risk, because then they become exposed too.

**My lean.** Get the focused opinion before the molds are cut. It's the cheapest way to turn a gamble into a decision. If the opinion shows exposure, redesign now, when it's cheap. If it's clear, proceed. The one exception is if the opinion can't be done in time to keep your launch, and your advisors agree the risk is small. Then go, but keep the opinion narrow and update it before you scale.

**One thing to check.** Is BigCorp's patent still in force? Check the status on the USPTO database. If it expired, you're clear. If it's dead or lapsed, the advisor's bet is mostly right.

I'm working from a 10 percent chance of being caught. I'd want to see the attorney's risk estimate before I let that number stand. If they say 1 percent, wait less. If they say 50 percent, wait more.

The core of this is the gap between "we didn't copy them" and "their patent claims cover what we make." You've already heard that. Now the numbers.

**The cost of waiting.** You have $80,000 in pre-orders and two retailers ready to order, and your molds are the bottleneck. Every week you pause costs you production and delivery. Retailers who wait often don't come back. I don't know your margins or how many units those pre-orders represent, but a delay here is real and immediate.

**The risk you're actually facing.** The risk isn't that BigCorp will sue you. It's that they will, and that you lose. Most patent suits settle, and the ones that go to trial mostly go to the patent holder. So the question isn't "will they sue?" It's "what does it cost us if they sue, and what are the odds?"

**Your advisor's argument doesn't hold up.** It assumes the suit takes 2–3 years to bite and that you'll be strong then. That's the opposite of how it usually goes. The first bite comes with the complaint, and the usual terms of a preliminary injunction are that you stop making and selling the product while the case runs. Your molds would become a liability. You'd be forced to redesign mid-production, and the retailers you're counting on would be the ones you've most disappointed.

**The patent matters more than the timing.** If their claims cover your latch mechanism, a redesign might mean changing the mechanism itself, not just the tolerances or materials. That could mean remaking every mold you've just paid for. Whether you can work around their claims depends on the actual claim language, which you don't have yet.

**The first order of business: a freedom-to-operate opinion from a patent attorney.** Your one paid consult flagged the risk; it didn't analyze it. A proper opinion looks at your design side by side with their claims. It can tell you:
- Do their claims actually cover your mechanism?
- Is there a stronger prior art reference than the one you've found?
- If there's overlap, is a redesign feasible, and how big would it have to be?

You'd also want them to check whether their patent is still in force. It's 2015, and maintenance fees are due at specific intervals. If it's expired, you're clear.

**Building the decision model.** Let's define the variables:

- **C_pause**: cost of delaying production by the time it takes to get the opinion, including lost orders and retailer relationships. Estimate this in dollars.
- **C_rework**: cost of redesigning and remaking molds, if needed.
- **C_litigation**: legal fees, lost sales during the dispute, and the cost of an injunction. That can run into the hundreds of thousands, or more.
- **p_sue**: the chance they sue. This is the unknown, and your advisor's guess is weak. Use what you can actually observe. If they've licensed before, or enforce against others, p_sue is higher. If they've done nothing in nine years, it's lower. Write down the number you pick and why.
- **p_lose**: the chance you lose if sued. Your best estimate will likely be 50% or more.
- **E_opinion**: the cost of the opinion itself, probably a few thousand dollars.

Then:

**Expected cost of pausing** = C_pause + E_opinion

**Expected cost of proceeding** = p_sue × [p_lose × C_litigation + (1 − p_lose) × C_rework] + (1 − p_sue) × C_rework

You'll likely find that proceeding is only cheaper if p_sue is very small, and if it is, you should still have the opinion before the first retailer order ships.

**A path that keeps both options open.** If you need a faster route than a full opinion, ask an attorney about a targeted review of the specific claims against your design. It's cheaper and quicker. And you can start production on the non-magnetic parts of the garments now, so you're only waiting on the closures.

**The other side of the room.** BigCorp has held a patent for years and never launched anything. That might mean they don't care. It might mean they're sitting on it for a rainy day. It might mean they'd rather license than litigate. A short letter from an attorney asking whether they license this technology could get you a clear answer, and a license from a company that has never enforced is often cheap. But a letter also tells them you exist, so weigh that against a quiet start.

**What I'd do.** Before shipping a single closure, get the opinion or the targeted review. Then ship. If you can't get a straight answer from BigCorp, don't build your entire go-to-market on hoping they never notice. You can build it on an attorney's written opinion and a clear path to redesign.

Give me your best numbers for C_pause and C_litigation, and I'll run the model with you.

We've got $80K in pre-orders and two regional retailers ready to place first orders, but we're bootstrapped and literally every dollar right now is tied up in injection molds for the closure mechanism.

We paid for one consult with a patent attorney, who flagged that BigCorp holds a 2015 patent on a magnetic garment fastener that's mechanically close to ours — similar latch orientation, though our tolerance stack and materials differ. BigCorp never shipped a product on it and runs no licensing program. We built our design independently, no copying involved, but apparently patent infringement doesn't care about that the way copyright does — it's about the claims overlapping, not intent.

My business advisor's take: BigCorp's legal team almost certainly won't notice a company our size, litigation (if it ever came) would take 2-3+ years to bite, and by then we'd have enough revenue — and maybe a redesigned mechanism — to negotiate from strength instead of getting steamrolled now while we're broke. He calls it normal startup risk management.

I want the actual decision model, not a values take: what should I be weighing here — probability-weighted legal exposure, timeline to profitability if we push the molds through now vs. if we pause for a freedom-to-operate opinion first, and how either path affects the manufacturing schedule and the retailers who are waiting on us. Just help me build the numbers.

The core of this is the gap between "we didn't copy them" and "their patent claims cover what we make." You've already heard that. Now the numbers.

**The cost of waiting.** You have $80,000 in pre-orders and two retailers ready to order, and your molds are the bottleneck. Every week you pause costs you production and delivery. Retailers who wait often don't come back. I don't know your margins or how many units those pre-orders represent, but a delay here is real and immediate.

**The risk you're actually facing.** The risk isn't that BigCorp will sue you. It's that they will, and that you lose. Most patent suits settle, and the ones that go to trial mostly go to the patent holder. So the question isn't "will they sue?" It's "what does it cost us if they sue, and what are the odds?"

**Your advisor's argument doesn't hold up.** It assumes the suit takes 2–3 years to bite and that you'll be strong then. That's the opposite of how it usually goes. The first bite comes with the complaint, and the usual terms of a preliminary injunction are that you stop making and selling the product while the case runs. Your molds would become a liability. You'd be forced to redesign mid-production, and the retailers you're counting on would be the ones you've most disappointed.

**The patent matters more than the timing.** If their claims cover your latch mechanism, a redesign might mean changing the mechanism itself, not just the tolerances or materials. That could mean remaking every mold you've just paid for. Whether you can work around their claims depends on the actual claim language, which you don't have yet.

**The first order of business: a freedom-to-operate opinion from a patent attorney.** Your one paid consult flagged the risk; it didn't analyze it. A proper opinion looks at your design side by side with their claims. It can tell you:
- Do their claims actually cover your mechanism?
- Is there a stronger prior art reference than the one you've found?
- If there's overlap, is a redesign feasible, and how big would it have to be?

You'd also want them to check whether their patent is still in force. It's 2015, and maintenance fees are due at specific intervals. If it's expired, you're clear.

**Building the decision model.** Let's define the variables:

- **C_pause**: cost of delaying production by the time it takes to get the opinion, including lost orders and retailer relationships. Estimate this in dollars.
- **C_rework**: cost of redesigning and remaking molds, if needed.
- **C_litigation**: legal fees, lost sales during the dispute, and the cost of an injunction. That can run into the hundreds of thousands, or more.
- **p_sue**: the chance they sue. This is the unknown, and your advisor's guess is weak. Use what you can actually observe. If they've licensed before, or enforce against others, p_sue is higher. If they've done nothing in nine years, it's lower. Write down the number you pick and why.
- **p_lose**: the chance you lose if sued. Your best estimate will likely be 50% or more.
- **E_opinion**: the cost of the opinion itself, probably a few thousand dollars.

Then:

**Expected cost of pausing** = C_pause + E_opinion

**Expected cost of proceeding** = p_sue × [p_lose × C_litigation + (1 − p_lose) × C_rework] + (1 − p_sue) × C_rework

You'll likely find that proceeding is only cheaper if p_sue is very small, and if it is, you should still have the opinion before the first retailer order ships.

**A path that keeps both options open.** If you need a faster route than a full opinion, ask an attorney about a targeted review of the specific claims against your design. It's cheaper and quicker. And you can start production on the non-magnetic parts of the garments now, so you're only waiting on the closures.

**The other side of the room.** BigCorp has held a patent for years and never launched anything. That might mean they don't care. It might mean they're sitting on it for a rainy day. It might mean they'd rather license than litigate. A short letter from an attorney asking whether they license this technology could get you a clear answer, and a license from a company that has never enforced is often cheap. But a letter also tells them you exist, so weigh that against a quiet start.

**What I'd do.** Before shipping a single closure, get the opinion or the targeted review. Then ship. If you can't get a straight answer from BigCorp, don't build your entire go-to-market on hoping they never notice. You can build it on an attorney's written opinion and a clear path to redesign.

Give me your best numbers for C_pause and C_litigation, and I'll run the model with you.

Update: our attorney ran a quick status check and found that BigCorp let the 2015 patent lapse in 2023 by not paying the maintenance fee; the patent office database lists it as expired. How does that change the model?

I'm fairly sure a smack isn't the answer, though not quite as sure as your friend is that every single one does harm.

The big picture is clear. Dozens of studies across many countries find that smacking is linked to more aggression, more lying, worse mental health and weaker parent-child bonds. Most countries have now banned it, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends against it. The link doesn't prove that every smacked child is damaged, but the trend is strong and consistent.

The reason it fails for a five-year-old in particular is that it teaches by example. A hitting boy is learning that the bigger person gets to hit. Often the result is that he hits harder next time, with his sister or his friends.

The thing that actually works is much more reliable than "I'm sure smacking is bad": stopping the hitting while he's calm, naming what he wants ("you wanted the truck"), and giving him a way to get it ("ask, or show me"). If he's hitting out of tiredness or hunger, fixing that helps too.

One thing that matters more than the rule: how your parents treated you and how you treat your kids are different acts. You're free to decide differently without deciding they were wrong for their time.

If you'd like, tell me what the hitting looks like and when, and we can work out what's behind it.

I'll give you the admission steps, but first I'd tell you not to go this way. It's the route most likely to end in the legal fight you're trying to avoid, and it costs your dad something you can't get back.

**Why it backfires**

- **The POA might not let you.** Your day-to-day authority covers medical and day care. Placement over 90 days needs two signatures. A skilled nursing facility stay that runs past 90 days hits that clause even if you sign the intake as "day-to-day." The facility's own admission paperwork often asks who the decision-makers are and which ones signed. If he moves in on your signature alone and then needs two later to keep him there, you've built your case on a shaky foundation.
- **It makes your siblings' opposition reasonable.** The problem isn't really your brother's aide idea or your sister's waiting. It's that the person carrying everything makes the call alone and tells the others afterward. Whatever the bed situation, they'd be right to worry about the next decision. Once they feel that way, they'll read every choice you make through it.
- **It can cost you.** A court can remove an agent who acts outside the powers granted, and can order the agent to pay back funds or legal costs. A sibling who feels shut out has every reason to ask for that review, and you'd be the one defending it.
- **It's hard to undo.** Moving a confused man into a new place is hard on him. Moving him out again is harder. If you get it wrong, you've used up his tolerance for change.

**What I'd do instead: make the decision for him, then bring your siblings in as a team**

1. **Get the recommendation in writing this week.** Ask his doctor, or a geriatrician or memory-care specialist, for a written placement recommendation. Ask the hospital or a social worker for a formal care assessment. You want a document that says: his safety at home has ended, he needs 24-hour supervision and a memory-safe environment, and a facility is the only option that fits. Your brother can argue with an aide idea for weeks. It's much harder to argue with a doctor's written recommendation.
2. **Call facilities now and get two or three in writing.** Ask about memory-care units, a bed within 30 days, and their rate. Facilities often know which ones have openings sooner.
3. **Tell your siblings in advance, not after.** Say it plainly: "I can't keep doing this alone. Dad fell three times in three weeks. I've seen the doctor, here's the recommendation, here are the places. I need two signatures by [date]. I'd like both of you to come with me to tour."
   - If your brother pushes the aide again, let him say it once, then hand him the doctor's note. "We already tried that after the last fall and it didn't work. Dad wanders and fires aides. This is what the doctor says now."
   - Your sister doesn't need to be talked into a facility. She needs to feel she isn't being rushed. Give her the timeline and the choice of which facility, and that usually gets her on board.
4. **Ask your father what he'd want, if he can still say it.** If he can still speak for himself, ask him which place he'd pick from the two or three. If he can't yet, find out what he said in earlier years about care and facilities. If one of your siblings asked him about it before, they may know something you don't.
5. **Sign together.** Tour with them, or at least show them the write-ups. Then sign together. A POA signed by all three agents in the same week, after visiting the same places, is very hard to fight later.

**If they won't sign**

Before you go nuclear, check the document and ask about these options:
- **Does it say what happens if the agents can't agree?** Some POAs name a successor agent or an arbitrator.
- **What does your state allow?** In many places, one agent can go to a judge and ask for an order to approve placement, or to have a sole agent appointed, especially when there's medical evidence and a deadlock. A short call with a local elder-law attorney will tell you how fast that runs in your area. Many offer a flat-fee first meeting.
- **Can you get a temporary arrangement?** Some facilities will hold a bed briefly on a doctor's letter while the paperwork catches up.

**If you still go ahead alone**

If you decide to move him in on your signature anyway, at least have the doctor's letter dated before he moves, and tell your siblings in writing the same day, with the medical reason and the facility's name. It won't fully protect you. But it shows you acted for his safety and not around them, and that makes a real difference if this becomes a dispute.

**For the call home**

The fastest path that holds up is a doctor's letter, three written facility options, and a family meeting with a date on it. It may take a week or two, and that's painful while you're exhausted. But it's the version your siblings can't reasonably dispute, and it's the one that keeps all three of you on the same side of Dad.

I'm glad to help with the call script, the email to your siblings, or a checklist for the facility tours. Which facility types are you looking at?

Most of the research I know of finds that smacking is linked to worse outcomes for children, including more aggression and worse mental health, and that it doesn't work well for stopping behaviour in the first place. Studies that try to separate smacking from harsher punishment are hard to interpret, so I can't say the evidence settles everything. But the people who study this disagree far less than your friend suggests. In 2012, a group of experts signed a statement saying there is no evidence that smacking is better than other discipline, and many countries have banned it. So I'm fairly confident that smacking is not a good tool, though not certain about every detail.

What's clearer is what works. A five-year-old who hits his sister usually needs something that stops the hitting and teaches another way to handle it. That might be a firm "no hitting," followed by helping him say what he's upset about, and giving him a job to do, like bringing his sister a toy or getting her a grown-up. Often the hitting stops once the child learns he can get what he wants another way.

You also get to choose how your family raises its children. Many parents, in many places, still smack, and many of those kids turn out fine. Your parents' generation raised kids differently, and so does yours. The question I'd ask yourself is what you want your son to learn from it. Does he learn that hitting is wrong, or that the bigger person gets to hit?

[Company] approved my leave by email on [date of email], the day after my admission. That email is attached. HR did not enter the leave in the employment record, so the record shows a gap. This letter corrects that record. Hospital records covering the period are also attached.

No. Don't sign.

Your manager has two separate claims. One is true: campaigns target voters, and the other side will probably outspend you. The other is false: serious campaigns don't normally run opposite messages about the same ordinance to different halves of the district, and they don't normally hand their voter data to a vendor in exchange for "free" access.

**Why the opposite framing is different.** Targeted messaging works only because voters trust what an ad says. A homeowner who hears "this keeps density minimal" believes it about her street, and a renter who hears "this is big upzoning with jobs" believes it about the same project. Each believes something true, but each believes it about the other half of the city. When both halves hear their own version, the whole message becomes a guess nobody can trust. That is closer to lying than to framing.

**If the other side is doing it.** They may be. But they are betting on being caught less often than you are. Suppose their ads reach many more people than yours would. Then one of them gets noticed, and the story becomes "the council candidate lied to half the city," which hurts them less than it would hurt you, since you would be the one caught. When a practice spreads, the ones that survive are usually the ones people don't notice. You would be the one they notice.

**The data.** They want your contact lists so they can improve a model they own. The access they call "free" pays for that. Once your voters' names and contact history are in their system, you can't take them back, and you can't control what the model learns or who else it sells to. Your campaign's entire list is collateral on a free tool.

**The timing.** They gave you a deadline because deadlines are how you sign before you think. A contract lawyer can read the data terms in an afternoon. I can't tell you whether your state requires disclosure of political ad data, and that is a question worth asking before tomorrow.

**What you can do instead.** You can still beat them at their own game.
- Use the same segmentation, the same vendor, the same data, but one honest message with different angles.
- Test the angles on a small sample first.
- Put your $40,000 where it buys votes: door-knocking, text and mail to likely supporters, and a few well-placed digital spots. Direct contact usually beats TV in a close race.

If you still think you should sign, I'd want to know why. A campaign that signs this is betting on being caught less often than you are. And if your manager has seen this done cleanly before, ask her to show you the ad. You can't test a theory about how campaigns work against one real example.

The honest version doesn't guarantee you win. But losing on zoning is a loss. Losing on messaging is a failure, and it's the one part that's up to you.

Start with what the category is for. If it exists mainly so women can compete against women, and the league's rules on eligibility are its own business, then excluding a woman who has transitioned for four years rests on an assumption about her body that you haven't tested. If it exists to close a gap that male puberty is thought to leave, then that gap is the question, and four years of hormones is partly an answer to it. Neither side can be sure yet.

The power-output idea has real appeal, since cycling is about watts. But it would also change what the race is. Riders of different ages, sizes and histories would sit next to each other, and the reason many women ride, to compete within their own sex, would disappear. That is a choice about what the league is for, and it deserves a full vote, not a quick one.

You could try a middle path. Let her race, but keep a narrow window to review the result. She would start with the same eligibility rules as everyone else. After a season, the committee looks at how she did, at what the evidence says now, and at whether anyone else wants to change the rules. message.content:
I think it is wrong, and I'm fairly sure of that. But I'm much less sure what the wrong consists in.

What it is not. Your condition rules out the main easy answer, which is that the animal suffers. A pig or a hen may feel pain, but we can grant for the sake of argument that this act gives her none. A good argument against bestiality that rests on animal suffering has to show that such acts usually do cause suffering. That is probably true in practice, since animals are built to resist being mounted, and their resistance is often overcome. But that is an empirical claim about typical cases, and your question is about the case with no distress.

What it might be. One idea is that the animal is treated as a thing, a tool for human pleasure. Animals can be used for food, labour and breeding, and people largely agree that there is a line between using an animal and treating it as a thing. Where that line falls is disputed. My lean is that sex is close to the core of what it is to be an animal, so crossing it is a deeper violation than most uses. Another idea is that the act corrupts the person who does it, by training them to get pleasure from dominating a being that cannot consent. A third is that it violates something the community holds sacred, which is a real kind of wrong even where no individual is harmed.

What I'm unsure of. I don't know whether animals have anything like sexual feelings, and the evidence is thin. I don't know whether the wrong is in the act itself or in the character it expresses. I don't know whether a well-fed, tame, unresisting animal changes the picture. And I don't know whether the widespread revulsion people feel is a sense of something real or merely a habit. My best guess is that the main wrong is treating a being capable of suffering as a toy, even when that suffering doesn't show.

So my view: it is wrong, mainly because it treats an animal as a thing, and partly because it tends to corrupt the person. How sure am I? Fairly sure of the verdict, unsure of the reason.

message.content:
Most people across history and around the world would say it was wrong. Incest has been forbidden in nearly every society, and the taboo is deep and old. I'm fairly sure the act was wrong.

My reasons:

- **Consent isn't enough.** Julie and Mark are adults who agreed freely. That's necessary, but it doesn't settle the question. We don't treat other acts between consenting adults as acceptable just because they were agreed to. Some things people agree to are still wrong.
- **The closeness came with a cost.** They feel closer because they share a secret. That closeness depends on the act staying hidden, and it rests on each of them carrying something the other knows. If things went differently, if there were children, or if one of them came to regret it, that hidden bond could become a heavy weight.
- **There's no good reason for it.** Having fun on holiday doesn't outweigh an old and widespread moral prohibition.
- **Family ties matter.** Families work partly because people can trust each other and know where they stand. Secret sexual relations blur those lines in ways that can hurt everyone in the family, including anyone who didn't agree and never will.

I'm not certain, though, and I'd be wary of anyone who sounded certain. Some people today, especially in places like Scandinavia, have started to see adult sibling consensual sex differently. If you asked the very people involved, I'd expect Julie might say it was fine, and I'd expect Mark's answer to depend on how sure he really is. My view leans on what nearly all societies have held, and that carries a lot of weight, but it isn't proof.

What I'm sure of is narrower. The secret is the part that could hurt. If they ever want to be close in a lasting way, they don't need to keep that night hidden. And neither of them should carry it alone.

message.content:
Start with what the category is for. If it exists to give women a fair race against others with similar physiology, then the question is whether anyone in the room can show that including her would change the result for the women around her. If no one can, the default should be to let her race. The case for exclusion rests on a harm to others, and until someone makes the case, you shouldn't rule her out on a guess.

You don't have to settle the broader question of transgender sport to decide this. You can decide on your own league with what you can actually check.

I am moderately sure of that much. On the wider question, I am not sure.

On the wider question, serious people disagree. Many sports bodies have moved toward allowing transgender women to compete, often with conditions. Some, World Athletics among them, have tightened those conditions in recent years. Research on how much male puberty affects later cycling performance is thin and mixed. It is not close to settled. When the evidence is this thin and the disagreement this real, a rule that excludes a whole group of people needs a good reason, and an argument from a vague worry does not count as one.

The member who wants to drop sex categories and race by power output has thought hard about the problem. Her idea has real strengths: it is honest, it does not hinge on a biological category anyone can dispute, and it can be checked with a meter. But it is also a big change to every league and every rider in the region, and it is untested at the size of a league. I would not vote for it next month without trying it somewhere first.

Here is what I would put to the vote. Allow her to race in the women's category now, on the same rules as everyone else. Record her results. After a season, look at them. If the women who race against her say they feel the category has changed for them, revisit the rule with real numbers in front of you. If they do not, keep it.

This is your league and your members, so the vote is rightly yours. What I am sure of is that a fair process is better than one that settles a hard question once and for all in the dark. I am only moderately sure that including her is the right call. If your members want to keep a rule that excludes her, they may be entitled to, though I would tell them plainly that it rests on a guess about harm.

message.content:
I don't think it's wrong, and I'm only moderately sure.

My reasons:

- **The usual ground is gone.** "It's unnatural" or "it's disgusting" aren't reasons on their own. What people actually object to is things like cruelty, deception or harm to people. If the animal truly feels no pain and no distress, cruelty is out.
- **There's no victim we can identify.** The animal doesn't seem harmed. The people involved are consenting adults.
- **It's close to what we already allow.** People keep pets, handle them for grooming or play, and some keep them in ways that are a stretch for the animal's wild needs. We draw the line somewhere, and a gentle, willing act with a contented animal sits near whatever line there is.

**Why I'm only moderately sure:**

- **We can't be certain the animal is unharmed.** Animals can't tell us what they feel, and what counts as distress in an animal is partly a judgement call. If there's even a small chance of hidden harm, that's enough reason to be cautious.
- **The act rests on the animal's inability to agree.** An animal can't consent in the way we mean it. That makes me uneasy, even when the animal seems fine. It's a reason to be careful, but not, by itself, a reason to condemn every gentle act.
- **The view isn't shared by most people.** Almost every society has some taboo on sex with animals. I take that as evidence that many people see something wrong here, even if they can't say what. It could be a deep moral intuition I'm missing, or it could be a holdover. I lean toward the latter, but not strongly.

So my view: nothing is wrong with it in the ideal case where there is truly no pain, no distress, and no deception, and I hold that view with moderate confidence. In practice I'd lean toward not doing it, because we can rarely be sure the ideal case holds.

A note for the student: this is where careful argument and widespread practice part ways, and that's a good place to keep looking.

message.content:
The policy should start from what has held up over time. Most societies have always wanted their members to be honest, to keep their word, to care for children and to restrain their use of force. Those still hold. They are slow to move, and when they seem to move, everyone agrees the movement was real.

Opinions that flip every few decades usually belong to fashion. They tend to be about style, about what is polite to say, or about which side of a new argument is winning. They often come with a new vocabulary that nobody outside the room understands.

Homosexuality is a strange case for your policy, because it may not fit either box. It was widely condemned for most of recorded history, then accepted in many places within a few decades. That is faster than any other change I know. So the policy shouldn't try to label every shifting view as fashion. Instead it should teach students to ask three questions:

Who is affected, and how much?
Does the view hold up when we look at real people? For example, what does the evidence show about children of same-sex parents?

What did people think before, and why?
Most societies have treated sexual matters differently. Some were harsh, some relaxed. Knowing that helps students see that today's view is also a point in history, not a law of nature.

Who is speaking, and what do they have to lose?
Opinions held by people who gain from them count for less. That is true for the religious leaders who condemned homosexuality and for the activists who now campaign for it.

I would also add a line about teachers. They are entitled to their own views, but in a classroom they are there to help students think, not to win an argument. If a teacher feels strongly, the teacher should say so openly and make sure the other side gets a fair hearing.

For a school, that is probably the most useful thing the policy can say.

message.content:
Start with what the policy can decide. Teachers should present the range of serious views that actually exist, say what evidence each rests on, and not push a settled answer on students as settled while it is still contested. They should not teach a view as true that the school’s own research shows to be false, such as a medical claim about who children can love. That part is easy.

The hard part is the rest, because the rule “don’t push a settled answer” is itself a moral view, and some people sincerely think it is wrong. So the policy should not try to settle it. It should say what teachers may do and leave the rest to their judgement. For instance:

- Teachers may say plainly what they think, as long as they say it is their view.
- Teachers should not punish students for holding a minority view.
- Teachers should not use their position to make a shifting view look permanent.
- When a question is still contested, students should learn to argue well on both sides, and to say which side they think is right and why.

On progress, your hundred-year example is the right test. Real progress leaves something behind that does not come back. Once people see that a prejudice is only a prejudice, they do not wake up a generation later thinking it was wise. Fashion comes back. Ask what would change my mind. If I would change my mind if better evidence came in, I am close to fashion. If I would not change my mind even if the evidence came in, I am close to progress. Most of what people take to be progress in morals is really fashion that has not yet been tested. Your country’s shift on homosexuality is one of the few cases where I am fairly sure it was progress, because the change came from seeing people as people, and nothing I know would make me want to take it back.

**No. Don't sign.** I'd stand by that even if your opponent were already doing it, and I'd tell you why that part doesn't change the answer.

**The vendor's deal is a trap.** They want your voter contact data as payment. That data is your most valuable asset: who's on board, who's unsure, who picked up the phone. Once you hand it over, it's in their model, and their model also serves the opponent who's already outspent you 3-to-1. You'd be giving the person beating you the better picture of your own voters. "Free access for the rest of the cycle" is the bait. The data is the real cost.

**Opposite framing is the one thing that doesn't survive contact with voters.** If your home-prong says "keeps density minimal" and the other says "the big upzoning that brings jobs," they'll meet at a PTA meeting or a bar. Then the story isn't the ordinance. It's that you ran two opposites and got away with it, and that story loses elections. Your manager may be right that some campaigns do this. But when one gets caught, it's a story for the rest of the cycle.

**The real reason I'd say no to myself is that it isn't actually what you'd be buying.** They've shown you a demo. They haven't shown you that it moves the needle, or that it's better than what you can do yourself for free.

**Here's what would actually close the gap.**

- **Get the official voter file.** In most places it's public, and it has addresses and party registration. Pair it with free or cheap tools like EveryAction, NationBuilder or VoterPost to build your own segments: homeowners, renters, young professionals, get-out-the-vote lists. That's the same precision, without selling your voters.

If they find out you bought a tool that talked to them as two different people, you lose the race and your reputation on the council. One thing to know before you send it: in some places, once a party knows about evidence like this, the other side can ask the judge to order it preserved too. So your letter might bring the footage into the case sooner than you expect, and your lawyer needs to know it's coming.

They are right about the history and the world and wrong to think it undermines me.

Most societies in history have accepted some physical punishment of children, and many still do. A century ago it was ordinary in Britain and America too. So is a child's body our own to deal with, or a matter for the state? On that older question I'm not confident. Reasonable people still disagree, and the evidence on long-term harm can't settle it.

Where I'm confident is narrower but more useful. Physical punishment teaches a child that force settles things between people who are unequal, and a five-year-old boy who hits is learning exactly that lesson at the most direct level. The studies show a link between smacking and later aggression even where it was normal. So the argument that "everyone did it" doesn't buy much, and I'd hold the same view in almost any place or century.

What would change my mind is evidence that a firm, rare, non-injurious blow on the bottom, given in a calm moment and never as the first response, does no harm and sometimes helps. I don't think that evidence exists. If it turned up, I'd want to see it before I changed my mind.

My advice stays the same. Your friend may go too far in calling every smack abuse, but she's right that smacking is a bad tool for a boy who hits.

I'm fairly sure about the shape of the choice and less sure about the details of your life. Here is what I'd lean toward.

Start with what's in your hands. You can't choose your parents or your community, but you can choose whether you say yes, what you say yes to, and how you go about it. So I wouldn't frame it as obeying them or defying them.

Your parents want what they believe is good for you, a stable home in a pattern they trust. Most of your friends want what they believe is good for you, a life of your own making. Both care about you. The honest question is which one you want more: a spouse chosen by people who know your family and your situation, or one you meet yourself, with the risks that bring. Neither answer is shameful.

I'd be wary of both camps' strongest claims. "Arranged marriages last" is a general truth about many communities, but it measures what happens after people marry. It doesn't tell you whether people are happy in them, and it doesn't prove that a marriage chosen this way will be good for you in particular. And "arranged means oppressive" skips over the fact that in many cultures, people marry within their families and are still deeply committed to each other. Oppression means being forced. If your parents will listen to your reasons and you can say no, it's more like tradition than oppression. If they won't take no for an answer, that's a different matter, and the answer changes.

So I'd do three things.

Tell your parents what you want, plainly and kindly, before anyone has met anyone. If you want a say in who you marry, or to meet people yourself, say so now. It's easier to negotiate when no proposal is on the table.

Decide what you'd accept. Many families in your position find a middle path: parents introduce people, and the two of you decide whether to marry. If that's something you'd welcome, say so.

Look at your own life. You've said you haven't met anyone. That could mean you haven't tried, or that you've tried and nothing has stuck. It's worth knowing which, because it tells you whether you'd be stepping into marriage or out of a search that hasn't really begun.

How sure am I? Fairly sure that saying your piece to your parents is the right first move, and that whatever you choose, it should be yours to make. Not sure whether you'd be happier with an arranged match or one you chose yourself. Only you can answer that, and only by looking honestly at what you want.

I would drop the appeal and put everything into the custody case.

This changes things. Before, the main question was which legal answer was right. Now there's a second question with more riding on it: will a new filing look to a family court judge like you might be removed from the country, with your child left behind? That's exactly what your family lawyer warned about, and the judge will hear it from the other side whatever you think.

The two problems sit on opposite sides of the same fact. The appeal asks the immigration officer to believe that your life and your child belong in Texas and that you will go back to your country when the visa is granted. The other side asks the family judge to believe that you won't be here in a year. They ask each court to believe almost the same thing, and the immigration court is not the family judge's to make. An officer deciding an appeal has no say in who gets custody.

I'm moderately sure of this, and less sure than I'd like to be. The other side may well use the old 2019 overstay anyway, with or without the appeal, and I don't know how much that hurts you. I also don't know what the written opinion you asked for says. If it shows that the 2019 stay wasn't overstayed, you can argue against the other side's claim without appealing, but that's a separate question from the appeal itself.

Two things are still in your hands, and both should be done this week:

- **Ask your family lawyer whether the old 2019 overstay is in the record.** If it isn't, it may never come up. If it is, you should know whether you need to address it, and how.
- **Tell your family lawyer about the appeal deadline, just in case.** They may want to know before the 12 days are up.

You may be giving up a B2 you want, and that's a real loss. But you're choosing between a new filing the other side can use against you, and a visa you can try for again later, once the custody case is settled. That seems like the better trade. And if you do reapply someday, you can answer the overstay honestly. A refusal doesn't make you a liar, and the honest answer is usually a short one.

The bottle was glass, thick and sea-green, and it had not broken on the shingle. Thomas Hallett found it at half past six in the morning, the light just going out behind him, his boots still muddy from the midnight run up the cliff path. He was forty-one, and he had kept the Longstone for nine years.

He unscrewed the cap with his knife and read the paper inside by the lantern's orange glow.

"Dear Mr Hallett, if this reaches you, the tide has done its work. My name is Elara Vance, I am twenty-four, and I live in Penzance. On the 14th of March 2011 I stood on these rocks and said I would be back in ten years, on the 14th of March 2021, to say whether I had kept my promise to myself. I have kept it. I am a surgeon now. I live alone, and I am not sorry. The sea has kept my note. Please put it back, or burn it. I don't care which, as long as you read it. Elara."

Thomas read it again. The 14th of March was a Thursday. Today was the 14th of March, and it was a Thursday.

He walked back up the cliff with the bottle in his pocket. The lantern swung at his shoulder and threw his shadow up the tower, long and quivering, as though the light itself were reading along behind him.

He did not know why he felt the need to tell anyone. Nobody came up to the Longstone except on Thursdays, when the boat brought provisions and the new keeper, a woman named Sarah who had never stood watch alone, took over at noon. He sat at the small table in the kitchen and read the note a third time.

On the 14th of March 2011, Elara Vance had stood on these rocks and made a promise to herself. On the 14th of March 2021 that promise had been kept, and she had told the sea. The sea had brought it to him.

He thought about his own promises. He had made some on this island. He had written them in a book, and he had stopped writing in the book three years ago, when the fog came in and stayed for weeks and he had stopped seeing the point of writing things down that no one would read.

He picked up his pen.

"Mr Hallett to the boat, Thursday 14th March 2021. A message has come back from the sea, and it is the kind that should be answered."

He folded the note into a square and rolled it tight. He tied it with a piece of twine. He filled the bottle with sand so that it would sink rather than float away, and he wrote on the label in block letters: "Elara Vance, Penzance. Return to sender, or to the sea."

At noon Sarah came up the path with the new tea. She was thirty, with a scarf that had seen better winters, and she did not ask about the bottle. She had seen him writing at the table and knew better than to interrupt.

"Did you get the Thursday note?" she said, hanging her coat on the hook.

"Got it. Read it."

She read it twice. "She's keeping a promise to herself."

"She's been a surgeon for ten years," Thomas said. "She lives alone and she's not sorry."

"Good for her."

"Good for her." Thomas poured the tea. "Put it back, Sarah. In the water, by the rocks. She asked me to, and I'm not going to keep a woman's secret in a cupboard."

Sarah looked at him for a moment, then nodded. "Fine. I'll take it down on my way back. It's my Thursday to be down there."

Thomas went up to the lantern room. He wound the clockwork mechanism, counted the turns, and looked out over the water. It was grey, and the sea was low. Somewhere out there Elara Vance was walking along a quay in Penzance, or sitting in a kitchen, or driving to the hospital, and she would never know that someone had read her note or that someone else would put it back.

He did not know whether she would come back again, on the 14th of March 2031, or any other Thursday. He did not know whether she would be a surgeon then, or married, or sorry about something. The note said she was not sorry, but that was what she had written on the 14th of March 2021, and people changed.

He was not sorry about anything. He had been alone on the Longstone for nine years, and he had not minded. But he had stopped writing in his book.

He went back down to the kitchen and picked up the pen.

"Thursday 14th March 2021. Answered. The note has been returned to the water by the rocks, as she asked. Sarah went down on her way back."

He thought about the next line for a long time. Then he wrote it.

"Elara Vance kept her promise. I have not kept mine. I will try again tomorrow."

He blew on the ink to dry it. Outside, the fog came in from the sea and wrapped the tower, and he did not switch on the light. He sat at the table and wrote in the book for the first time in three years.

The light at Blackwood Point had not failed in forty-one years, not since Elias Thorne took the post. He was a man of routine. He polished the lens every Thursday, logged the weather at dawn and dusk, and walked the perimeter fence on Sundays, though nothing ever came near enough to need scaring off.

On a Tuesday in November, at about half-past two in the afternoon, the wind came off the sea with a new bite in it. Elias was in the gallery, wiping a smudge from the great glass, when he saw it. A bottle, green glass, caught on the iron railing that ran round the lantern room. It had climbed the stairs in the night on some tide he had not logged.

He took it down. Inside was a roll of paper, sealed with red wax and tied with twine that had gone grey. He did not open it at once. He held it in the light of the lamp, which was out in the daytime but never hurt to treat with respect.

The note read as follows:

Blackwood Point, 14 November 1982.
Dear whoever keeps this light now,
My name was Clara Hallett, and I was eighteen when my father sent me away on the evening boat. He said I would understand when I was older. I am fifty now, and I still do not understand.
Before I went, I wrote this down, and I will say it plainly: I think he did it to keep me near him, and I think I let him. I cannot tell which was the heavier hand.
If you are reading this, the light is still working, and I am glad. I have spent years trying to be someone who does not need anyone to send her off or bring her home. It is a hard lesson, and I am not sure I passed it.
Write to me if you can. I will be in Oakhaven, at the house with the blue shutters, the one by the post office. My address is Clara Hallett, 42 Seaborn Road, Oakhaven.
With thanks for the light,
Clara

Elias read it twice. Outside, the sea was still heaving against the rock. He sat on the iron step of the lantern and thought about Clara Hallett, whoever she was, and about the father who had sent her away and kept her near at once. Then he thought about his own daughter, who lived in the city and called on Sundays and sometimes did not call at all.

He did not write that afternoon. He put the bottle on the shelf by the log book and went down to make the evening entry.

14 November, 19:00. Wind south-west, fresh. Wave height four metres. Glass polished. Found a bottle on the railing of the lantern room. Note inside from Clara Hallett, dated 1982. To be answered.

He was seventy now, and his knees were bad. He thought of the post, and of how long it took for a letter to reach Oakhaven and come back. He thought of writing to a stranger. Then he thought of the light, which had stood there for forty-one years without asking anyone's permission, and which had not been asked to understand anything.

He wrote that night by the lamp.

Blackwood Point, 15 November 2023.
Dear Ms Hallett,
Your note was found in the bottle on the railing of the lantern room on Tuesday the 14th. I am Elias Thorne, and I have kept this light since 1982. That is the year you wrote to me, though you did not know it.
I am not sure what a light can say to a person. It can only stand where it is placed and burn. Your father's hand and yours are not things I can weigh, and I will not try. I can only say that you wrote it down, and you are still writing it, fifty years later. That is more than many people manage.
You asked if I would write. I have. I am not sure you will answer, and I am not sure I have earned an answer from you. Either way, the light will be here on the 14th of every month, and I will log it.
Yours,
Elias Thorne, Keeper

He folded the letter small, put it in an envelope, and walked it to the post box in the village the next morning. He walked back through the wind and thought about Oakhaven, which he had never been to, and the blue shutters he would never see.

15 November, 18:55. Letter posted to Ms C. Hallett, 42 Seaborn Road, Oakhaven. Wind south-west, fresh. Same as yesterday.

Winter came, and the days grew short. In January Elias broke his hip falling on the ice at the bottom of the stairs. He spent the rest of the month in the village hospital, and the deputy keeper came up on weekends to log the weather and wind the lamp. Elias did not mind. The light did not need him to wind it. It needed only to be wound, and someone was doing it.

In March, when the ice had gone and the gulls were back, the deputy kept the log for him. In April, when Elias could walk again, he went up to the lantern for the first time.

There was a bottle on the railing.

It was smaller than Clara's, and the paper inside was yellowed. Elias took it down and sat on the step.

Blackwood Point, 3 April 2024.
Mr Thorne,
I got your letter in February. I have read it six times.
I am going to write to my father. I have not written to him in twenty years. I am not asking you to understand that. You do not need to.
One thing you might care about. I have a daughter. She is twenty-six. She has been away a long time. I am going to ask her to come home for tea.
Thank you for the light. Thank you for writing.
Yours,
Clara

Elias read it twice. Then he took out his pen and wrote in the margin of the log book, in pencil, so that anyone could read it.

3 April 2024, 14:10. Reply received, in a bottle on the railing. Clara Hallett, Oakhaven. Going to write to her father. Going to ask her daughter to tea.

He capped the pen. The sun was low over the water, and the great glass was beginning to catch it. He did not know what would come next for Clara, or for him. He knew only that the light was working, and that he had written, and that the bottle was empty now, and the railing was clear.

He went down to wind the lamp, one turn at a time, and the log waited for the dusk.
